newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Kabila road plan to open up Democratic Congo.
newsitem.headline: Kabila road plan to open up Democratic Congo.

text.p: Democratic Congo's President Laurent Kabila has embarked on priority objectives of opening up his huge country with a planned $2.5 billion road programme and reinforcing links with neighbours.
On Wednesday Kabila wrapped up summit talks with leaders of Uganda and Rwanda, two neighbours who helped him seize power in May and who are now central to his economic calculations.
The summit agreed to send envoys to the European Union to revive a loan for regional roads, notably rebuilding of the 500-km (300-mile) Goma-Kisangani road, a communique said.
On the eve of the summit's opening on Tuesday, Planning Minister Babi Mbayi said Kabila's government would rebuild or rehabilitate 28,000 km (17,500 miles) of roads over three years.

Opening up a country the size of Western Europe is estimated to cost $2.5 billion for roads alone. A road network left by Belgian colonial rulers at independence in 1964 disintegrated under dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, who ruled for 32 years.
Babi said the programme would be 60 percent financed internally and the rest through external sources.
Public Works Minister Bishikwabo Tshiumbaka told reporters that if external financing was not forthcoming, Congo could shoulder the entire cost without aid. He did not elaborate.
Asked who the contractors would be, he said: "We haven't got to the stage of deciding who would carry out the work."
One idea floated by Kabila's ministers is to tie potentially lucrative mining contracts into infrastructure projects.
Kabila targeted roads and communications, partly because of widespread belief that Mobutu neglected the sector as a deliberate policy to keep his people perpetually uninformed.

The renamed Democratic Republic of the Congo is blessed with a vast interior water transport network notably the massive Congo River. A rail line linking copper and cobalt mining centres in southern Shaba Province and South Africa was improved by private management but is not serviced by feeder roads.
"The three heads of state discussed roads infrastructure and communications links between the east of our country (Congo) and the west of their countries," a joint summit communique said.
"It was decided to send a common delegation this month to revive a loan which was approved for the reconstruction of this road," Kabila told reporters.
An EU mission announced last week that Brussels was ready to resume cooperation with the ex-Zaire after a five-year freeze amid charges of misrule by ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko.
There were no details of any EU loans or the estimated cost of the road project at today's valuation.
"It is a principal route which is going to serve the three countries," Kabila said, expanding on a joint communique.
The road from Goma on Lake Kivu to Kisangani, the third largest town in Democratic Congo, gave Kabila's guerrillas vital access to the interior.
Kabila's forces seized power in Kinshasa in mid-May after the ailing Mobutu fled to Morocco via Togo.
This week's summit followed growing signs that international donors are prepared to give Kabila the benefit of the doubt over human rights and democracy, key conditions for aid.
A senior World Bank official said last week that donors were ready to work with Kabila's Congo because its revival is crucial to the fortunes of other states in central Africa.

Other donors are resuming operations, despite worries about human rights under Kabila and the country's big debt arrears to multilateral agencies. It owed $474 million in arrears to the African Development Bank alone at the end of 1996.

"You really need to look for the countries that have the size and resource endowment necessary for a sub-region," Jean-Louis Sarbib, one of the World Bank's two vice-presidents for Africa told Reuters in an interview.
He said that without a Congo that is a vibrant economy "very little is going to happen in Central Africa".
Donors are due to meet Kabila's representatives in September or October, focusing on rebuilding the country and setting up, effectively from scratch, an administrative structure, he said.
Apart from the road projects, Congo and Uganda agreed separately to embark on a joint search for oil around Lake Albert and Lake Edward, which form part of their borders.

In a symbolic sign of the new era of trade links betwween Uganda and Congo, two neighbours kept apart by mutual suspicion in the Mobutu era, Ugandan companies mounted a modest exhibition this week in Kinshasa.
After the summit, Museveni toured the stands displaying mainly household utensils inside the former parliament, idle now since Kabila banned political activity after his takeover.
